title: Bartik shift-share IV for local employment shock on wages

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
Instrumental Variables (IV) using Bartik shift-share instrument. The instrument exploits variation in predicted local employment growth based on national industry trends and local industry composition. Key assumptions: (1) Exclusion restriction - national industry growth affects local wages only through local employment, not directly; (2) Relevance - the instrument predicts local employment growth; (3) Exogeneity - national industry shocks are uncorrelated with local wage determinants after controlling for observables.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load required libraries
library(AER)
library(stargazer)

# Read the data
data <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s22_data.csv")

# Check data structure
print("Data summary:")
summary(data)

# First stage: regress employment growth on instrument and controls
first_stage <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = data)
print("\n=== FIRST STAGE RESULTS ===")
print(summary(first_stage))

# Check instrument relevance (F-statistic)
f_stat <- summary(first_stage)$fstatistic[1]
print(paste("First-stage F-statistic:", round(f_stat, 2)))

# Reduced form: regress wages on instrument and controls
reduced_form <- lm(y ~ z + controls, data = data)
print("\n=== REDUCED FORM RESULTS ===")
print(summary(reduced_form))

# Two-stage least squares (2SLS) estimation
iv_model <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = data)
print("\n=== IV (2SLS) RESULTS ===")
print(summary(iv_model))

# Extract key coefficient
iv_coeff <- coef(iv_model)["x"]
iv_se <- summary(iv_model)$coefficients["x", "Std. Error"]
print(paste("\nMain Result: Employment elasticity of wages =", round(iv_coeff, 3)))
print(paste("Standard error:", round(iv_se, 3)))
print(paste("95% CI: [", round(iv_coeff - 1.96*iv_se, 3), ",", round(iv_coeff + 1.96*iv_se, 3), "]"))

# OLS for comparison
ols_model <- lm(y ~ x + controls, data = data)
print("\n=== OLS COMPARISON ===")
print(paste("OLS coefficient:", round(coef(ols_model)["x"], 3)))
print(paste("IV coefficient:", round(iv_coeff, 3)))

# Robustness checks
print("\n=== ROBUSTNESS CHECKS ===")

# Check for weak instruments
if(f_stat < 10) {
  print("WARNING: Weak instrument (F-stat < 10)")
} else {
  print(paste("Instrument appears strong (F-stat =", round(f_stat, 2), ")"))
}

# Hausman test for endogeneity
hausman_stat <- summary(iv_model)$waldtest[1]
hausman_p <- summary(iv_model)$waldtest[4]
print(paste("Hausman test statistic:", round(hausman_stat, 3)))
print(paste("Hausman test p-value:", round(hausman_p, 3)))

# Alternative specification without controls
iv_no_controls <- ivreg(y ~ x | z, data = data)
print(paste("IV coefficient without controls:", round(coef(iv_no_controls)["x"], 3)))

print("\n=== FINAL RESULT ===")
print(paste("A 1% increase in local employment growth increases wages by", 
            round(iv_coeff*100, 1), "percentage points"))
```

## 3. Expected Findings
I expect a positive coefficient around 0.3-0.8, indicating that a 1% increase in employment growth increases wages by 0.3-0.8 percentage points. This reflects standard labor demand elasticity - employment shocks should increase wages through tighter labor markets. The IV estimate should be larger than OLS if there's measurement error in employment or if unobserved negative productivity shocks simultaneously reduce both employment and wages (creating downward bias in OLS). The Bartik instrument should be relevant (F-stat > 10) since local industry composition creates predictable variation in employment responses to national industry trends.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: IV/2SLS — Bartik shift-share instrument; identification from national (exogenous) shifts
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Employment growth driven by national shifts raises local wages
